claim: The Met signature is more effective than the satellite signature in distinguishing ERMS from ARMS in two large panels of human primary RMS.
source: Interestingly, in both datasets the Met signature was more effective than the satellite signature in distinguishing ERMS from ARMS (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 1A using two datasets (Davicioni et al., 2009; Williamson et al., 2010)

claim: The Met score is higher in RMS compared to muscle.
source: The Met score was higher in RMS compared to muscle (Figure 1B)
evidence: Supported by box-plot analysis in Figure 1B showing statistical significance (p<0.0001)

claim: The Met score is higher in ERMS rather than ARMS.
source: The Met score was higher in RMS compared to muscle (Figure 1B) and in ERMS rather than ARMS (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by box-plot analysis in Figure 1C showing statistical significance (p<0.01 and p<0.0001)

claim: The first top quartile of patients with high Met score is enriched in ERMS samples.
source: Interestingly, only by using the Met score the first top quartile was enriched in ERMS samples (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by ranked distribution analysis in Figure 1D showing statistical significance

claim: There is a significant overlap of ERMS samples with both high Met and satellite scores in the top quartiles.
source: However, in the top quartiles there was a significant overlap of ERMS samples with both high Met and satellite scores (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by Venn diagram analysis in Figure 1E showing statistical significance (p<0.05 and p<0.0001)

claim: The Met score is significantly enriched in UPS compared to other sarcomas.
source: Interestingly, the Met score was significantly enriched in UPS compared to other sarcomas, while the fibroblast signature distinguished UPS from RMS (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: Supported by box-plot analysis in Figure 1F showing statistical significance (p<0.001)

claim: The fibroblast signature distinguishes UPS from RMS.
source: Interestingly, the Met score was significantly enriched in UPS compared to other sarcomas, while the fibroblast signature distinguished UPS from RMS (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: Supported by box-plot analysis in Figure 1G showing statistical significance (p<0.0001)

claim: MH mice are born at the expected Mendelian frequency.
source: MH mice, born at the expected Mendelian frequency, showed normal postnatal muscle growth (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Direct statement about breeding outcomes

claim: MH mice show normal postnatal muscle growth.
source: MH mice, born at the expected Mendelian frequency, showed normal postnatal muscle growth (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by body weight measurements and images in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: Expression of Hgf and eGFP is restricted to skeletal muscle and is Dox-dependent in MH mice.
source: Expression of Hgf and eGFP was restricted to skeletal muscle and was Dox-dependent (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: Supported by fluorescent imaging and RT-PCR analysis in Figure 2B,C

claim: HGF is measurable in transgenic muscle but undetectable in blood.
source: While HGF was measurable in transgenic muscle, it was undetectable in blood (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by HGF-ELISA quantification in Figure 2D

claim: MH mice show a modest reduction of fiber size compared to control littermates.
source: Muscle sections showed a modest reduction of fiber size (Figure 2E,F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by cross-sectional area distribution analysis in Figure 2E,F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C showing statistical significance (p<0.01)

claim: MH mice have a higher number of satellite cells compared to control littermates.
source: However, Pax7 immunofluorescence revealed a higher number of satellite cells compared to control littermates (Figure 2G,H).
evidence: Supported by Pax7 quantification in Figure 2G,H showing statistical significance (p<0.001)

claim: More Pax7-positive cells are detected on freshly isolated single myofibers from MH mice.
source: More Pax7-positive cells were also detected on freshly isolated single myofibers (Figure 2I,J).
evidence: Supported by quantification in Figure 2I,J showing statistical significance (p<0.05 and p<0.001)

claim: At time 0, some satellite cells in MH mice are MyoD-positive, indicating basal activation.
source: Surprisingly, at time 0 some satellite cells were MyoD-positive, indicating basal activation (Figure 2K,L).
evidence: Supported by MyoD quantification and immunofluorescence in Figure 2K,L showing statistical significance (p<0.01 and p<0.001)

claim: The differences in satellite cell activation in MH mice are Dox-dependent.
source: These differences were Dox-dependent (Figure 2I,K) and lasted for three days in culture (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: Supported by comparison of Dox-treated and untreated conditions in Figure 2I,K

claim: Myofibers isolated from MH mice contain more myonuclei than controls.
source: Furthermore, myofibers isolated from MH mice contained more myonuclei than controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by myonuclei quantification in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F showing statistical significance (p<0.01)

claim: MyoD-positive cells are detectable in transgenic muscle sections, indicating the presence of activated satellite cells in vivo.
source: MyoD-positive cells were also detectable in transgenic muscle sections (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G), indicating the presence of activated satellite cells also in vivo.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G

claim: Homozygous deletions of the CDKN2A locus have been reported in the majority of human tumors including sarcomas.
source: Homozygous deletions of the CDKN2A locus has been reported in the majority of human tumors including sarcomas (Miller et al., 1997; Roussel, 1999; Ruas and Peters, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Miller et al., 1997; Roussel, 1999; Ruas and Peters, 1998)

claim: More than 17% of UPS exhibit loss of the CDKN2A locus according to CGH analysis.
source: Specifically, CGH analysis revealed that more than 17% of UPS exhibited the loss of the locus, while up to 39% of the UPS did not express the corresponding p14 protein (Pérot et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Pérot et al., 2010)

claim: Up to 39% of UPS do not express the p14 protein.
source: Specifically, CGH analysis revealed that more than 17% of UPS exhibited the loss of the locus, while up to 39% of the UPS did not express the corresponding p14 protein (Pérot et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Pérot et al., 2010)

claim: The deletion of the CDKN2A locus occurs in 32% of UPS cases.
source: The frequent inactivation of the locus has been confirmed by an additional study (Simons et al., 2000) reporting the deletion in 32% of UPS cases.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Simons et al., 2000)

claim: The genetic inactivation of the CDKN2A locus in RMS has been extensively reported.
source: Furthermore, the genetic inactivation of the CDKN2A locus in RMS has been extensively reported (Chen et al., 2007; Obana et al., 2003; Paulson et al., 2011; Seki et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Chen et al., 2007; Obana et al., 2003; Paulson et al., 2011; Seki et al., 2015)

claim: Approximately 30% of all MHI-null mice display an apparently hypertrophic phenotype.
source: Approximately 30% of all MHI-null mice displayed an apparently hypertrophic phenotype (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: Supported by images and distribution data in Figure 3A-C

claim: All MHI-null mice with hypertrophic phenotype quickly develop tumors.
source: All of these mice quickly developed tumors and the histology revealed a picture of multistage progression (Figure 3D, stage 1 to 4).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis in Figure 3D

claim: The histology of tumors in MHI-null mice reveals a picture of multistage progression.
source: All of these mice quickly developed tumors and the histology revealed a picture of multistage progression (Figure 3D, stage 1 to 4).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis showing stages 1-4 in Figure 3D

claim: In the periphery of MHI-null tumors, proliferating satellite cells surrounding old fibers are mixed with more mature MyoD- and Myogenin-positive cells.
source: In the periphery of the tumor (Figure 3D, stage 1) proliferating (Ki67-positive) satellite cells, surrounding old fibers, were mixed with more mature MyoD- and Myogenin-positive cells.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical analysis in Figure 3D, stage 1

claim: At early stages of MHI-null tumor development, Pax7-positive cells are detectable beneath the basal lamina of newly formed fibers.
source: At this early stage, Pax7-positive cells were detectable beneath the basal lamina of the newly formed fibers, suggesting that satellite cells retained the ability to return to quiescence (Figure 3E, right panel).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence in Figure 3E, right panel

claim: Satellite cells in early stage MHI-null tumors retain the ability to return to quiescence.
source: At this early stage, Pax7-positive cells were detectable beneath the basal lamina of the newly formed fibers, suggesting that satellite cells retained the ability to return to quiescence (Figure 3E, right panel).
evidence: Inferred from the presence of Pax7-positive cells beneath the basal lamina

claim: The central area of MHI-null tumors consists of tissue with high cellularity and no evidence of terminal myogenic differentiation.
source: The central area of the tumor consisted of tissue with high cellularity and no further evidence of terminal myogenic differentiation (Figure 3D, stage 4).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis in Figure 3D, stage 4

claim: The tumor bulk in MHI-null mice is eGFP-negative indicating that the cells are undifferentiated.
source: Accordingly, the tumor bulk was eGFP-negative indicating that the cells were undifferentiated (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by fluorescent imaging in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: The histological markers and anatomical localization of MHI-null tumors are compatible with the ERMS subtype.
source: The histological markers (Pax7, MyoD and Myogenin, Figure 3D, stage 4) and the anatomical localization (trunk, neck and occasionally the orbit) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), were compatible with the ERMS subtype.
evidence: Supported by histological analysis in Figure 3D and anatomical localization in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: MHI-null mice develop tumors with a short latency of 3.95 months.
source: MHI-null mice developed tumors with a short latency (3.95 months), while mice heterozygous for the Cdkn2a locus (MHI-het) showed delayed tumor formation (6 months) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier survival curve in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C

claim: MHI-het mice show delayed tumor formation at 6 months.
source: MHI-null mice developed tumors with a short latency (3.95 months), while mice heterozygous for the Cdkn2a locus (MHI-het) showed delayed tumor formation (6 months) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier survival curve in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C

claim: The majority of tumors in MHI-het mice have lost the wild type Cdkn2a allele.
source: PCR analysis revealed that the majority of the tumors in MHI-het mice had lost the wild type allele (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by PCR analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D

claim: Tumor development in MHI-null mice maintained under Dox treatment until P10 occurs with the same latency and incidence as mice not treated with Dox.
source: In this cohort of mice, tumor development occurred with the previously described latency and incidence (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier survival curve in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C

claim: Fetal myoblasts are not involved in ERMS development in MHI-null mice.
source: To exclude the involvement of fetal myoblasts in ERMS development, MHI-null mice were maintained under Dox treatment until P10. Given the persistence of Dox in the tissues, transgenic Hgf and eGFP expression became detectable from day 40 onward (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B), when only resident muscle stem cells are present. In this cohort of mice, tumor development occurred with the previously described latency and incidence (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Inferred from the experimental design where Dox treatment until P10 excludes fetal myoblasts but tumors still develop

claim: Pax7-deficient C57/B6 mice are viable at birth but progressively die in 2-3 weeks.
source: Pax7-deficient C57/B6 mice are viable at birth, but progressively die in 2–3 weeks (Mansouri et al., 1996; Seale et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Mansouri et al., 1996; Seale et al., 2000)

claim: In Pax7-deficient mice, the number of satellite cells is reduced at birth and further declines during postnatal development.
source: In these mice the number of satellite cells is reduced at birth, and further declines during postnatal development.
evidence: Statement about the phenotype of Pax7-deficient mice

claim: Between 5 and 10% of Pax7-deficient mutant animals in a mixed genetic background survive into adulthood.
source: However, in a mixed genetic background, between 5 and 10% of mutant animals survive into adulthood (Oustanina et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Oustanina et al., 2004)

claim: The mixed genetic background has no effect on sarcoma incidence and latency in MHI-null P-null mice.
source: The mixed background had no effect on sarcoma incidence and latency (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier survival curve in Figure 4B

claim: MHI-null P-null mice show a drastic reduction in ERMS incidence.
source: However MHI-null P-null mice showed a drastic reduction in ERMS incidence (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by penetrance and histological distribution data in Figure 4C

claim: Less than 30% of MHI-null P-null tumors are positive for MyoD and Myogenin and are classified as ERMS.
source: Notably, immunohistochemistry revealed the positivity for MyoD and Myogenin in less than 30% of cases, which were classified as ERMS (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical analysis in Figure 4C,D

claim: The majority of MHI-null P-null tumors (more than 70%) are classified as UPS due to complete absence of tissue-specific markers of differentiation.
source: Interestingly, the majority of tumors (more than 70%) presented extensive cellular heterogeneity from round to spindle-shape cells, with nuclear appearance ranging from hyperchromatic to pleomorphic. The complete absence of tissue-specific markers of differentiation categorized these tumors as UPS (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical analysis in Figure 4C,D

claim: Both UPS and ERMS tumors in MHI-null P-null mice express Met.
source: Accordingly, while both UPS and ERMS tumors expressed Met, only UPS were positive for the pan-fibroblast marker PDGFRα (Figure 4D,E)
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical and Western blot analysis in Figure 4D,E

claim: Only UPS tumors in MHI-null P-null mice are positive for the pan-fibroblast marker PDGFRα.
source: Accordingly, while both UPS and ERMS tumors expressed Met, only UPS were positive for the pan-fibroblast marker PDGFRα (Figure 4D,E)
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical and Western blot analysis in Figure 4D,E

claim: UPS tumors from MHI-null P-null mice are Sca1-positive and Integrin-α7-negative, indicating a mesenchymal-like phenotype.
source: and FACS analysis on freshly isolated tumors revealed that they were Sca1-positive and Integrin-α7-negative (Figure 4F), indicating a mesenchymal-like phenotype (Driskell et al., 2013; Guarnerio et al., 2015; Joe et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis in Figure 4F and citations to published literature (Driskell et al., 2013; Guarnerio et al., 2015; Joe et al., 2010)

claim: ERMS tumors from MHI-null P-null mice are Sca1-negative and Integrin-α7-positive, confirming the myogenic identity of this subtype.
source: In contrast, the ERMS were Sca1-negative and Integrin-α7-positive, confirming the myogenic identity of this subtype.
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis in Figure 4F

claim: Perturbation of the SC niche microenvironment can give rise to distinct sarcoma subtypes in a Pax7 lineage-dependent manner.
source: Altogether our data clearly indicate that perturbation of the SC niche microenvironment can give rise to distinct sarcoma subtypes in a Pax7 lineage-dependent manner, and provide evidence for a fibroblast cell origin of UPS.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of tumor subtypes in Pax7 wild-type vs. null backgrounds

claim: UPS originates from fibroblasts.
source: Altogether our data clearly indicate that perturbation of the SC niche microenvironment can give rise to distinct sarcoma subtypes in a Pax7 lineage-dependent manner, and provide evidence for a fibroblast cell origin of UPS.
evidence: Inferred from the increase in UPS incidence in Pax7-null background and PDGFRα positivity

claim: Transgenic Hgf in the model comes from differentiated muscle fibers.
source: In our model transgenic Hgf comes from differentiated muscle fibers.
evidence: Statement about the model design

claim: The tumor mass is no longer exposed to transgenic HGF due to lack of differentiated muscle cells.
source: Thus the tumor mass is no longer exposed to transgenic HGF for lack of differentiated muscle cells, as shown by the absence of expression of the eGFP reporter in the tumors (see Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by fluorescent imaging showing absence of eGFP in tumors in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: Dox-mediated Hgf downmodulation does not impair tumor growth.
source: Accordingly, Dox-mediated Hgf downmodulation did not impair tumor growth (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B) indicating that transgenic HGF production was not essential for tumor maintenance.
evidence: Supported by tumor growth curve in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: Transgenic HGF production is not essential for tumor maintenance.
source: Accordingly, Dox-mediated Hgf downmodulation did not impair tumor growth (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B) indicating that transgenic HGF production was not essential for tumor maintenance.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Dox-mediated Hgf downmodulation does not impair tumor growth

claim: All primary murine tumors retain basal Met expression.
source: Although all primary murine tumors retained basal Met expression, in a subset of ERMS (which later turned out to be Met-amplified), Met was present at much higher level and overexpression was accompanied by receptor phosphorylation (Figure 5A,B, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot and immunohistochemical analysis in Figure 5A,B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B

claim: In a subset of Met-amplified ERMS, Met is present at much higher level and overexpression is accompanied by receptor phosphorylation.
source: Although all primary murine tumors retained basal Met expression, in a subset of ERMS (which later turned out to be Met-amplified), Met was present at much higher level and overexpression was accompanied by receptor phosphorylation (Figure 5A,B, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot and immunohistochemical analysis in Figure 5A,B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B

claim: At earlier stages of tumor development, paracrine HGF stimulation promotes Met receptor downregulation.
source: On the other hand, at earlier stages, paracrine HGF stimulation promoted receptor downregulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A) and this resulted in a difficult detection of Met and phospho-Met (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A

claim: The only human ERMS sample where Met expression rose above all others (#2083) harbors MET amplification.
source: The only ERMS sample where Met expression rose above all others (#2083) was found to harbor MET amplification (Shern et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data in Figure 5C and citation to published literature (Shern et al., 2014)

claim: A human ERMS case (INT291) carries MET amplification as shown by FISH analysis.
source: Interestingly, another example of human ERMS carrying MET amplification emerged from an independent FISH analysis of a small set (8 cases) of ERMS (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by FISH analysis in Figure 5D

claim: Murine and human data indicate considerable variability of Met expression and rare Met amplification.
source: Overall murine and human data indicate a considerable variability of Met expression and rare Met amplification.
evidence: Inferred from the combined analysis of murine and human data showing variable Met expression

claim: Met activation is detected in three ERMS cell lines (#187R, #1640 and #1796), representing 17% of the total panel.
source: Met activation was detected in three cell lines (#187R, #1640 and #1796, 17% of the total) (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A,B) that all turned out to be sensitive to Met inhibition (see below).
evidence: Supported by RTK phosphoarray analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A,B

claim: CGH analysis reveals amplification of the Met locus in three ERMS samples (#1640, #1671 and #187R).
source: Comparative genomic hybridization (CGH) revealed amplification of the Met locus in three samples (#1640, #1671 and #187R), and gain of the entire chromosome 6 in another one (#1796) (Figure 5E, Figure 7H).
evidence: Supported by CGH analysis in Figure 5E and Figure 7H

claim: CGH analysis reveals gain of the entire chromosome 6 in ERMS sample #1796.
source: Comparative genomic hybridization (CGH) revealed amplification of the Met locus in three samples (#1640, #1671 and #187R), and gain of the entire chromosome 6 in another one (#1796) (Figure 5E, Figure 7H).
evidence: Supported by CGH analysis in Figure 5E and Figure 7H

claim: Treatment of #1640 and #1796 cell lines with PHA-665752 results in abrogation of Met signaling.
source: Treatment of #1640 and #1796 cell lines (#1671 cells were unfortunately lost) with the Met-specific inhibitor PHA-665752 (herein referred as PHA) resulted in the abrogation of Met signaling (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A

claim: Treatment of #1640 and #1796 cell lines with PHA-665752 results in arrest of cell proliferation.
source: Treatment of #1640 and #1796 cell lines (#1671 cells were unfortunately lost) with the Met-specific inhibitor PHA-665752 (herein referred as PHA) resulted in the abrogation of Met signaling (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), in the arrest of cell proliferation (Figure 6A,B)
evidence: Supported by proliferation analysis in Figure 6A,B

claim: Treatment of #1640 and #1796 cell lines with PHA-665752 results in accumulation of cells in the G0/G1 phase of the cell cycle.
source: Treatment of #1640 and #1796 cell lines (#1671 cells were unfortunately lost) with the Met-specific inhibitor PHA-665752 (herein referred as PHA) resulted in the abrogation of Met signaling (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), in the arrest of cell proliferation (Figure 6A,B), in the accumulation of cells in the G0/G1 phase of the cell cycle (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Supported by cell cycle analysis in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B

claim: Treatment of #1640 and #1796 cell lines with PHA-665752 results in impairment of anchorage-independent growth.
source: Treatment of #1640 and #1796 cell lines (#1671 cells were unfortunately lost) with the Met-specific inhibitor PHA-665752 (herein referred as PHA) resulted in the abrogation of Met signaling (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), in the arrest of cell proliferation (Figure 6A,B), in the accumulation of cells in the G0/G1 phase of the cell cycle (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), in the impairment of anchorage-independent growth (Figure 6C)
evidence: Supported by soft agar growth assay in Figure 6C

claim: Treatment of #1640 and #1796 cell lines with PHA-665752 results in induction of apoptosis.
source: Treatment of #1640 and #1796 cell lines (#1671 cells were unfortunately lost) with the Met-specific inhibitor PHA-665752 (herein referred as PHA) resulted in the abrogation of Met signaling (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), in the arrest of cell proliferation (Figure 6A,B), in the accumulation of cells in the G0/G1 phase of the cell cycle (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), in the impairment of anchorage-independent growth (Figure 6C) and in the induction of apoptosis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by apoptosis assessment in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C

claim: The rare surviving cells after PHA-665752 treatment are fully differentiated.
source: Interestingly, the rare surviving cells were fully differentiated (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by MHC expression analysis in Figure 6D

claim: Crizotinib administration to mice with palpable tumors blocks ERMS growth and reduces tumor volume without symptoms of toxicity.
source: Crizotinib administration to mice with palpable tumors blocked ERMS growth and reduced the tumor volume, without symptoms of toxicity (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by tumor growth curve in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D

claim: Some ERMS cases have mutated phosphatidylinositol 3 kinase A (PIK3CA).
source: Accordingly, some ERMS cases of mutated phosphatidylinositol 3 kinase A (PIK3CA) have been reported (Chen et al., 2013; Shern et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Chen et al., 2013; Shern et al., 2014)

claim: 82.5% of RMS tumors display strong activation of the PI3K pathway.
source: and 82.5% of RMS tumors have been found to display a strong activation of the pathway (Renshaw et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Renshaw et al., 2013)

claim: LY 294002 dramatically reduces cell proliferation in ERMS cell lines #59 and #2320.
source: In two cell lines (#59 and #2320), LY dramatically reduced cell proliferation (Figure 6E,F)
evidence: Supported by proliferation analysis in Figure 6E,F

claim: LY 294002 strongly inhibits Akt phosphorylation in ERMS cell lines #59 and #2320.
source: In two cell lines (#59 and #2320), LY dramatically reduced cell proliferation (Figure 6E,F), strongly inhibited Akt phosphorylation, promoted accumulation in the G0/G1 phase of the cell cycle and induced apoptosis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E

claim: LY 294002 promotes accumulation in the G0/G1 phase of the cell cycle in ERMS cell lines #59 and #2320.
source: In two cell lines (#59 and #2320), LY dramatically reduced cell proliferation (Figure 6E,F), strongly inhibited Akt phosphorylation, promoted accumulation in the G0/G1 phase of the cell cycle and induced apoptosis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: Supported by cell cycle analysis in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F

claim: LY 294002 induces apoptosis in ERMS cell lines #59 and #2320.
source: In two cell lines (#59 and #2320), LY dramatically reduced cell proliferation (Figure 6E,F), strongly inhibited Akt phosphorylation, promoted accumulation in the G0/G1 phase of the cell cycle and induced apoptosis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: Supported by apoptosis assessment in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G

claim: The addiction to Met and PI3K are mutually exclusive in the tested ERMS cell lines.
source: PHA and LY did not interfere, respectively, with the proliferation rate of #59/# 2320 and #1640/#1796, confirming that these ERMS cells depend on the sustained activation of distinct signaling pathways (Figure 6A, B, E, F).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that PHA-sensitive cells are not sensitive to LY and vice versa

claim: Intratumoral heterogeneity is poorly reproduced in experimental models.
source: Intratumoral heterogeneity is poorly reproduced in experimental models.
evidence: General statement about the state of experimental models

claim: The model exemplifies intratumoral heterogeneity through isolation of a major Met- and a minor emerging Alk- or Kras-driven population from the same tumor.
source: Importantly, our model also exemplifies this feature, as shown by the isolation, from the same tumor, of a major Met- and a minor emerging Alk- or Kras-driven population.
evidence: Supported by the analysis of #187L and R cell lines showing different oncogene dependencies

claim: Expansion of Alk-driven population occurs following treatment with a Met inhibitor.
source: Expansion of the latter occurred following treatment with a Met inhibitor, underscoring the risk of drug-induced clonal evolution.
evidence: Supported by the observation that PHA-selected R cells become sensitive to Crizotinib and show Alk amplification

claim: #187R cells express high levels of phosphorylated Met while #187L cells do not.
source: Intriguingly, in the case of tumor #187 we obtained two cell lines (#187L and R), one of which (R) expressed high levels of phosphorylated Met while the other one (L) did not (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis in Figure 7A

claim: #187R cells are sensitive to PHA and Crizotinib.
source: R cells, as expected, were sensitive to PHA and Crizotinib (Figure 7C, D, F, G, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by proliferation, soft agar, and differentiation assays in Figure 7C, D, F, G and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C

claim: #187L cells are resistant to PHA but respond to Crizotinib.
source: Conversely, L cells were resistant to PHA but responded to Crizotinib (Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), suggesting amplification of Alk, a lesion frequently found in human RMS (van Gaal et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by proliferation assays in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, and citation to published literature (van Gaal et al., 2012)

claim: #187L cells express unusually high levels of ALK at baseline.
source: Indeed, while visualization of ALK protein by Western blot in the primary tumor extract required enrichment by immunoprecipitation (Figure 7B), L cells expressed unusually high levels of ALK at baseline (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis in Figure 7A,B

claim: In #187L cells, Crizotinib causes strong inhibition of ALK signaling, impairment of anchorage-independent growth, and induction of myogenic differentiation.
source: In L cells Crizotinib caused a strong inhibition of ALK signaling, impairment of anchorage-independent growth and induction of myogenic differentiation (Figure 7E–G)
evidence: Supported by Western blot, soft agar, and MHC staining in Figure 7E–G

claim: CGH and CNV analysis reveal Met and Alk amplification, respectively, in #187R and #187L cells.
source: Accordingly, CGH and CNV analysis revealed Met and Alk amplification, respectively, in R and L cells (Figure 7H, Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by CGH and CNV analysis in Figure 7H and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D

claim: Real-time PCR shows a low level of Alk expression in #187R cells, suggesting the original tumor contained a mixed population with a minor Alk-amplified component.
source: Interestingly, real-time PCR showed a low level of Alk expression also in R cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E), suggesting that the original tumor contained a mixed population with a minor Alk-amplified component.
evidence: Supported by real-time PCR analysis in Figure 7—figure supplement 1E

claim: PHA-selected #187R cells are negative for phospho-Met but sensitive to Crizotinib.
source: PHA-selected R cells were negative for phospho-Met (Figure 7I), but were sensitive to Crizotinib (Figure 7J).
evidence: Supported by Western blot and proliferation analysis in Figure 7I,J

claim: CGH, CNV and real-time PCR analysis reveal expansion of the Alk-amplified population upon PHA treatment of #187R cells.
source: CGH, CNV and real-time PCR analysis revealed the expansion, upon PHA treatment, of the Alk-amplified population (Figure 7H, Figure 7—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: Supported by CGH, CNV and real-time PCR analysis in Figure 7H and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D,E

claim: Prolonged PHA treatment of #1640 cells results in emergence of a clone harboring Kras amplification.
source: Conversely, prolonged PHA treatment of #1640 cells resulted in the emergence of a clone harboring also Kras amplification (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Supported by CGH and CNV analysis in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 3C

claim: The combination of Met and MEK inhibitors results in complete arrest of proliferation in PHA-selected #1640 cells.
source: Notably, the combination of Met and MEK inhibitors resulted in complete arrest of proliferation in these cells (Figure 7K).
evidence: Supported by proliferation analysis in Figure 7K

claim: The model demonstrates that selective perturbation of the SC niche results in distinct sarcoma subtypes in a Pax7 lineage-dependent manner.
